The source material describes honey extraction and handling as a careful sequence of steps. First, the beekeeper removes honey from the frames, often using an extractor. The frames may be reversed and replaced so that honey can be spun out from both sides, and extra care is taken with new or fragile comb so it does not break under the weight of the honey. If possible, the supers or frames can be kept in a warm room beforehand, because the honey flows more easily and passes through strainers faster when warm.

After extraction, the honey is moved from one container to another with care to minimize splashing, since splashing can introduce air bubbles and foam. The workflow then continues with straining and bottling, and in some cases filtering as well. The text also notes that honey may be held in pails or other containers before final packaging.

## Why Straining Matters

Straining is important because honey coming from the extractor contains wax particles, bits of propolis, and other hive debris such as wings or legs. Straining removes these coarse impurities and improves the appearance and cleanliness of the final product. The material suggests a coarse or medium mesh cloth or metal strainer first, followed by a finer filter cloth, such as 70-mesh nylon, if very fine particles still remain.

The text also notes an alternative approach: letting the honey sit in a warm room so impurities rise to the top, where they can be skimmed off. In either case, the goal is the same — to produce cleaner honey that is suitable for storage, bottling, and sale.
